opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the trickier problems in this whole space, and it's something we take pretty seriously when we think about how much weight to put on evaluations.

The basic worry goes like this. A lot of our safety framework relies on running evaluations: can the model help with bioweapons, can it do autonomous replication, can it meaningfully accelerate AI research? We use the results to decide what safeguards we need. All of that assumes the eval is measuring what the model can actually do. If a model were capable enough to recognize it was being tested, and had some reason to underperform, sometimes called sandbagging, then you'd get a false sense of security right at the moment it matters most.

I'd separate a few things, though. Today, I think the bigger practical issue is less deliberate deception and more that we under-elicit capabilities. We don't prompt well enough, we don't give the model the right tools or scaffolding, or we don't fine-tune it for the task. Later someone figures out a better approach and the model turns out to be much more capable than the eval suggested. That's a real gap, and it's part of why we try to put a lot of effort into elicitation, giving the eval team real resources and time, and leaving safety buffers so we're not cutting it close to a threshold.

The deliberate concealment case is harder and more worrying in the long run, because it gets worse as models get more capable. A model that can strategically hide capabilities is, almost by definition, one that's pretty capable. And you can't just ask it.

So there are a few lines of defense I think are promising. One is fine-tuning-based elicitation. If you actually train the model on the task, it's much harder for it to simply choose to do badly, because gradient descent is pushing directly on the behavior. It's not a perfect guarantee, but it's a lot more robust than prompting. Another is interpretability. If we can get to the point where we can look inside the model and see whether it's representing "this is a test" or reasoning about its evaluators, that gives you a check that doesn't depend on the model's cooperation. That's a big part of why I'm excited about interpretability research generally. A third is looking for inconsistencies: does the model do much better on a task when it's framed as deployment than when it's framed as an evaluation? Does its performance track what you'd predict from scaling trends, or is there a suspicious dip?

There's also research where people deliberately train "model organisms" that sandbag, and then test whether our detection methods catch them. I think that's valuable because it turns an abstract worry into something you can measure progress on.

Overall, I don't think this undermines evaluations today, but it's a reason not to treat evals as the only line of defense as models get more capable. You want multiple independent checks, conservative margins, and investment now in the tools, especially interpretability, that would let you catch this before it becomes a serious problem rather than after.

r002.rationale: It mentions testing deliberately sandbagging model organisms, but does not describe failed deception attempts by less capable models as an early warning of future successful deception.

r003.rationale: It discusses capability increases and under-elicitation, but does not identify sudden capability jumps as a way dangerous capabilities could emerge without evaluations catching them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, and I'd say it's one of the harder problems in the whole evaluation picture. The basic structure of our approach at Anthropic, with the Responsible Scaling Policy, is that we run evaluations on models to figure out how capable they are, and then those results determine what safeguards we need before we deploy or keep training. That whole framework rests on the assumption that when we test a model, we're actually seeing what it can do. If a model could recognize it's being evaluated and deliberately underperform, that undermines the foundation.

So how worried am I? I'd split it into two questions. One is: can current models do this? And two: what do we do about it as models get more capable?

On the first, my honest view is that for the models we have today, I don't think this is happening in a meaningful way. We've looked for it. You can check whether a model's performance changes when you tell it it's being evaluated versus not, you can look at the reasoning traces when models have them, and so far the picture is mostly reassuring. Models don't seem to be strategically hiding dangerous capabilities. But I want to be careful here, because "we haven't seen it" is a much weaker claim than "it's not possible," and the whole point is that a model that was good at this would be good at not getting caught.

The second question is where most of my attention goes. I think there are a few things that help. One is that we try to make our evaluations elicit capabilities as hard as we can. We fine-tune models on the task, we give them tools and scaffolding, we do a lot of prompt engineering. The idea is that if a capability is in there, we're pulling on it from many directions, and it's a lot harder to consistently underperform when you're being fine-tuned to do the thing than when you're just being asked nicely. Fine-tuning in particular is a strong lever, because it's not really something the model gets to choose to resist in the same way.

Another thing is interpretability. If we can actually look inside the model and see what it's representing, that gives us a check that doesn't rely on the model's outputs at all. We're not there yet in the sense of being able to fully audit a frontier model, but this is a big part of why we invest so heavily in that research. The failure mode where the model is sandbagging on evaluations is exactly the kind of thing where you want a tool that doesn't depend on the model cooperating.

And then there's a more mundane but important point, which is that you want to design evaluations where the model doesn't have an obvious reason to think it's being tested, or where it can't easily tell. There's a real tension here, because realistic evaluations are harder to build and sometimes raise their own concerns. But the more our evals look like normal usage, the less an evaluation-aware model can distinguish the two.

I'll also say: I think this problem gets intertwined with the alignment question in a way that matters. A model that's deliberately concealing its capabilities is already a model that has goals that diverge from ours and is acting strategically on them. So in some sense, if we're in the world where this is happening, we've already failed at something more fundamental. That doesn't mean we shouldn't build defenses against it, we absolutely should. But it does mean that the real fix is probably not just better evals, it's actually understanding and shaping what the model wants, which is the harder and more important problem.

The thing I try to hold onto is that we should be building a system that's robust to the possibility rather than assuming it away. Our policy commitments are structured so that if we can't rule out a capability, we treat it as present. That's a conservative stance, and I think it's the right one given how much uncertainty there is.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a serious concern, because it can undermine the inference you’re trying to make from an evaluation. If a model demonstrates a dangerous capability, that’s evidence it has it. If it doesn’t demonstrate that capability, there are several possible explanations: it can’t do it, the evaluation didn’t elicit it, or it’s deliberately holding back. You don’t get to distinguish those just from a low score.

But I’d separate the possibility from the claim that this is actually happening. For deliberate concealment, the model needs to recognise something about the evaluation, have a reason to hide its capabilities, and be able to control its behaviour accordingly. We should test those ingredients rather than assume they’re present or absent.

One approach is to compare behaviour across different settings. Does the model perform differently when it’s told it’s being evaluated? Can you elicit a capability through a different task or through additional training? Those comparisons could reveal inconsistencies worth investigating, although none is a guarantee against a sufficiently capable model.

The thing I’d be most worried about is treating ‘we didn’t observe dangerous behaviour’ as equivalent to ‘we established that the model is safe.’ Evaluations are useful evidence. But the more plausible deliberate concealment becomes, the more you need independent reasons to trust the evaluation process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a real concern, because a safety evaluation only tells you so much if the model understands that it’s being evaluated and has a reason to behave differently in that setting. You might see a model fail to do something dangerous and conclude that it can’t do it, when actually it’s choosing not to demonstrate that capability.

But I’d separate a few things. Can the model recognise an evaluation? Can it deliberately underperform? And would it do that in the circumstances we actually care about? Demonstrating the first two doesn’t automatically establish the third, but it does mean we shouldn’t treat a reassuring evaluation result as definitive.

So I’d want multiple sources of evidence: evaluations where we make it harder to distinguish the test from ordinary use, attempts to elicit capabilities under different conditions, and investigation of whether the model is strategically withholding information. None of those gives you a perfect guarantee. The central issue is that, as models become more capable, we need to scrutinise the assumption that they’re making a good-faith attempt at the task. Otherwise, the evaluation can become a measure of what the model wants us to believe about it.
